headline: Researchers at the Technical University of Munich have built a soft inflatable glove that reads forearm muscle signals and helps paralyzed hands grasp, letting one man with severe ALS hold a fork for the first time in four years.
score_reason: Pool 4 lowered by 2: the study was published in June 2026 and widely covered in early July, so this 12 Oct item is old news, and the result rests on one patient.
importance_line: A low-cost assistive glove gave a man with severe ALS back some everyday grip, which could matter to people with paralyzed hands from nerve disease, stroke or injury, but the result comes from one patient, the team says it is still adapting the design for others, and it is not yet a product.
source: Medical Dialogues, citing a Technical University of Munich study
summary: Medical Dialogues reports, citing a Technical University of Munich (TUM) study in Nature Machine Intelligence, that TUM researchers built a fabric glove with air cushions, inflated through 13 tubes, that bend each finger and turn the wrist when forearm sensors and machine learning detect that the wearer intends to grasp, which the researchers put at 97 percent reliability. In a test with a patient with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a disease that gradually destroys the nerve cells that control muscles, the system recognized his intention in 9 of 10 cases and he held a fork for the first time in four years; the study dates from June 2026, and the team says it is now adapting the glove for others, such as stroke survivors.
notes: Read in full via Medical Dialogues (fulltext). Old news re-dated: the paper appeared in Nature Machine Intelligence about 23 Jun 2026 and was covered widely on 6-8 Jul 2026 (Google News listings, headlines only); this is a 12 Oct 2026 re-run. The article's patient test shows an assistive robotic glove actually helping a person grasp, so machine_action is true.
